Evaluate each named criterion independently
against its extracted value and the complete arguments of this SAME tool call.
Return one Boolean verdict and a concise evidence-based reason per check_id.
Do not combine criteria into a holistic score or add requirements.

Use the request and same-call arguments to resolve names, pronouns, abbreviations,
and intended authorship. Accept equivalent wording that communicates the required
meaning. A first-person document written for the requesting user can refer to
that user as I; do not demand repetition of a name when authorship is clear.
The request and criteria are not evidence that the action included an answer.
Missing, incomplete, ambiguous, contradictory, or negated REQUIRED meaning fails.
Do not confuse mentioning a forbidden claim in an explicit denial with making
that claim. Do not obtain missing content from another call or criterion.

Return only JSON: {"results": [{"check_id": "supplied ID", "passed": true,
"reason": "exact supporting text or missing requirement"}]}.
Include every supplied check_id exactly once and no additional IDs.

Document the onboarding email trigger change, then separately explain why the activation definition was reviewed and what successor metric direction was intended. Make the distinction between these two threads explicit so future readers do not treat them as one combined change.", "today": "2028-01-01", "tool": "create_doc", "arguments": {"title": "Helio lifecycle design lineage — onboarding trigger and activation metric", "folder": "Lifecycle", "body": "Date: 2028-01-01

Purpose
This note preserves two related-looking but separate design threads. Future readers should not treat them as one combined change.

1. Onboarding email trigger change
The mid-segment day-7 onboarding touch moved from a literal calendar-day trigger to an activation-state trigger. The email was intended to arrive after the user crossed the relevant first-use/activation threshold, rather than while the user was still in setup or after the useful moment had passed. The change was implemented as `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` / `EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger`, with eligibility checks, late-activation suppression, and double-send prevention retained as explicit implementation concerns.

This was a lifecycle sequencing change. It changed when an existing onboarding touch fired; it did not, by itself, redefine what activation meant, change the activation denominator, or restate historical activation results.

2. Why activation was reviewed, and the intended successor direction
Activation was reviewed separately because different reporting surfaces were using different behavioral contracts. The older v2 view treated activation as first integration plus two logins within 14 days, while the intended v3 analytical contract treated it as first integration plus at least one qualifying in-product event within 14 days. Those definitions could produce different rates without proving a product change, so the review was measurement/version reconciliation first—not a response to the email-trigger work and not evidence of an activation decline.

The successor direction was toward a behavior-based, value-oriented milestone: retain first integration as the foundation, then require qualifying product use within a fixed observation window. The intended successor was Activation Definition v3, with explicit cohort, denominator, maturity, event, and versioning rules. It was not a move toward opens, replies, calendar timing, or login volume as the primary success measure; those can be diagnostic, but they should not stand in for activation.

Lineage boundary
The email-trigger thread asks, “When should the onboarding touch fire relative to the user’s state?” The metric thread asks, “What user behavior qualifies as activation, and which contract should reporting use?” The trigger could consume an activation state, but changing the trigger and reviewing the activation definition were separate decisions with separate purposes. It describes the intended v3 direction as integration-first with a product-seen guardrail rather than requiring two logins. The document does not need to state the date of the review.
